1.pericope_label: How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street
debates: What the gold and the holy stones stand for
Who the precious sons of Zion are
What occasion the poem laments
outliers: Henry takes the gold and stones of the temple and its overlaid gold and wrought stonework; Ellicott takes them for material treasures of palace or temple and nothing more; Clarke allows the temple but applies them particularly to the fallen priests and apostate prophets, the stones being godly men

Gill takes the sons for all the spiritual seed of the church and rejects the Jewish interpreters who make them a king and his children; Ellicott likewise refuses to confine the word to any class; Calvin restricts it to the chief men and royal counsellors, and Wesley and Clarke to nobles, priests and believers
Calvin denies that the poem laments the death of a king, since much in it does not suit that event, the enemy not having reached the city then nor the stones of the Temple been cast into the streets
Ellicott presses the verb as literally to be weighed with, so that the sons had been equal to their weight in fine gold
themes: Gold tarnished contrary to its nature, and stamped gold adulterated past passing
Stones of the sanctuary lying undistinguished among common ruins
A potter who remodels the vessel that does not please him
Jackals that give the breast where the mothers of the city would not

3.pericope_label: Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness
debates: What creature the sea monsters are
Whether the words for iniquity and sin mean punishment
Who is called cruel
outliers: Three readings of the creature: Gill settles on whales and cites Bochart and the ancients for their having breasts and milk; Clarke agrees but widens the word to all large and cruel creatures, aquatic or terrestrial; Ellicott gives jackals, noting the same word is elsewhere rendered dragons; Calvin makes them serpents

Calvin objects on grammatical grounds to taking the daughter of the people as the one called cruel, since the one word is feminine and the other masculine, and reads instead that the whelps of serpents are better used than this people

Keil and Delitzsch dissent from most expositors who give the words for iniquity and sin the sense of punishment, holding that meaning unestablished and that the scholar who argues for it has omitted a consecutive particle
Keil and Delitzsch reject two renderings of a phrase construed nowhere else with its preposition and prefer the sense of nibbling round something
themes: Paps hidden as in cases that must be drawn out
A curious rendering quoted from an old manuscript Bible
Dunghills that were heaps gathered for fuel instead of wood
Scarlet shawls of the rich exchanged for straw and rubbish

6.pericope_label: Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire
debates: Whether the words mean iniquity or punishment
Whether the separated ones are Nazarites or nobles
What the colours describe
outliers: Calvin allows both senses and takes punishment, since the verse dwells only on the grievousness of the suffering, and says he regards not what is plausible but what is true; Ellicott holds both words point to guilt rather than penalty, the greatness of the guilt being inferred from the suffering

Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and, as reported by Gill, many others take the word for nobles or princes, separated by dignity rather than by vow; Ellicott defends the traditional rendering outright, and Calvin, Gill and Jarchi keep the Nazarites

Clarke refers the lines to skin, flesh and veins, taking the sapphire for the veining because the verb means to intersect; Keil and Delitzsch reject a scholar who referred the whiteness to clothing; Ellicott would render the last word their form rather than polishing, and coral rather than rubies

Ellicott renders the clause about hands literally as none going round about her, meaning the destruction was the direct work of God and not of human agents; Clarke reports a rendering that hands were not weakened in her
themes: A doctrine that we may judge our sins by the greatness of our punishment
Abstinence from wine said to make a man pale, so that ruddiness is the more remarkable
Two pictures set side by side, the bloom of health and the spectral look of starvation
A word for blackness that may name a river dark with mud

9.pericope_label: They that be slain with the sword are better than they that be slain with hunger: for these pine away, stricken through for want of the fruits of the field
debates: How the clause about the fruits of the field should be read
Whether the last verse is hyperbole
Why the mothers are called pitiful
outliers: Ellicott reports a reading that refers the clause to men struck down in battle while fruits were still to be had, and rejects it, holding the construction of a psalm sufficient to support the received version; Calvin reports a reading that supplies a defect and prefers the more emphatic sense, that the produce of the earth took vengeance by refusing its usual supply

Ellicott grants the statement seems at first hyperbolical, since the city had twice been taken before, but explains it by later fortification and the failure of the attempt of Sennacherib; Keil and Delitzsch call it an overdrawn expression of deep subjective conviction that cannot properly be called hyperbole

All four voices take the word pitiful as deliberate contrast rather than praise, Calvin insisting it is no commendation but a mark of the madness that came upon women who would otherwise have been humane
Calvin presses the word foundations, since fire commonly takes the roofs and rarely penetrates so deep, and notes that where ruins remain there is at least an intimation of future restoration
themes: Sudden death called the easiest, against the languor of the faithful
A commentator who passes over the scene with as hasty a step as possible
A city whose capture appeared a miracle to those who knew its defences
A destruction that could not be ascribed to human forces at all

13.pericope_label: For the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her
debates: Who the blind are
How the clause about touching their garments should be read
Which prophets and priests are meant
outliers: Gill and Wesley take the blind for the prophets and priests themselves; Calvin refers the figure to the citizens at large, reading it of men who cannot distinguish and so touch a carcass or a diseased man unawares; Ellicott takes the blindness for a lust of blood or a hopeless despair

Calvin says interpreters have not understood the clause, rejecting the received rendering that they could not touch their garments as obscure and almost absurd, and the explanation of it as a warning to avoid contact with the unclean

Keil and Delitzsch report a dispute over the cry in the following verse, many rendering it as a shout raised about them rather than to them, since it was lepers who had to cry unclean and the warning went to the clean

Gill reports that Aben Ezra referred the words to the prophets of Baal and the priests of the high places, and holds instead that the false prophets and priests meant were those the people themselves had chosen and approved
themes: Watchmen of whose hands the blood of the flock is required
Righteous men said to be sacrificed to the idol of enmity against truth
A city where no corner was without a corpse, so that a man must pass on anyhow
Garments dripping with blood that men shrank from touching

15.pericope_label: The anger of the LORD hath divided them; he will no more regard them: they respected not the persons of the priests, they favoured not the elders
debates: Who cries unclean and to whom
Whose voice speaks of the anger of the Lord
Whether the last word means elders or old men
outliers: Gill and Ellicott have the people cry it to the blood-stained priests, reversing the law under which the leper cried it to those he met; Wesley reads it of the scrupulous crying to the rest to leave a city full of corpses; Calvin keeps it general and finds an allusion, he says unnoticed, to the law of the leper
Gill says expressly that these are not the words of the heathen continued but of the prophet; Wesley says they seem to be the language of the enemies triumphing over them

Keil and Delitzsch hold the word means not elders but old men, since it can only be referred to the priests and prophets already spoken of; Ellicott leaves the subject of the verbs to be supplied, whether enemies, heathen or men in general
Ellicott offers two renderings, that the eyes still waste away looking for a vain help, and that the watching is better given as upon a watch-tower
themes: Men who cleansed others of leprosy proclaimed unclean themselves
A promise of gathering set against a desolation in which nothing could be hoped
An abnormal form apparently copied from the verb that follows
Prosperity said to inebriate men so that they seek help here and there

18.pericope_label: The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD, was taken in their pits, of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen
debates: Who the anointed of the Lord is
Whether the hunting is done by Egypt or by the Chaldeans
What the phrase breath of our nostrils means
outliers: Gill and Calvin both reject the identification with the earlier king which the Targum and Jarchi give, and on the same grounds, that he fell in battle long before the city fell, was buried in the grave of his fathers, was not taken in pits, and that the kingdom did not cease with him; both name the last king of the line instead

Calvin reports that many apply the hunting to the Egyptians and prefers the Chaldeans; Keil and Delitzsch report the same dispute and note that two scholars set aside as strange and fanciful the idea of a third that Egypt is still in view
Calvin adds that the last king, however unlike his predecessor, was of the posterity of David and a type of Christ, and is called the anointed because his crown was not yet cast down

Ellicott takes the phrase for the breath of life and finds in it the ideal character of the king as the centre of the life of the nation, comparing a Roman writer who calls a ruler the vital spirit of his people
themes: Men who had no liberty in their own streets, much less to range the fields
A racer who dreamed he was an eagle and was told he would win
Two eagles released from east and west to find the middle of the world
A scheme of refuge with a friendly neighbour, rendered abortive by a capture

21.pericope_label: The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity: he will visit thine iniquity, O daughter of Edom
debates: Whether the call to rejoice is irony
Whether the closing promise was fulfilled
What the uncovering of sins means
outliers: Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Henry all take the call to rejoice as irony; Calvin reports this as the common reading and dissents, holding the clause states the summit of their misery, since nothing is harder to bear in wretchedness than the insults of enemies, with the consolation following after

Four readings of the promise: Gill divides its fulfilment between the seventy years and a later captivity; Clarke turns it forward to the Gospel and a gathering from all nations; Ellicott places it among unfulfilled prophecies, dependent on implied conditions forfeited by a later sin, though it held for five centuries; Calvin rejects the Jewish reading that refers it to a much later dispersion and holds the prophet meant only that the punishment would need no repeating
Clarke and Ellicott both read the uncovering by its opposite, since to cover sin is to forgive it and therefore to uncover it is to punish it

Henry is careful about the measure, that what is accomplished is not the fulness of punishment their iniquity deserved but of what God had designed, and that the troubles of his people last no longer than till they have done their work
themes: Lamentation psalms that end with light shining out of darkness
Enemies told to fill up the measure of their own iniquity
A people driven into all lands and expelled from a capital by edict
No call for a second exile where a land is already reduced to solitude
